opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the central issues, really. When we interact with a large language model through a chat interface, it's almost irresistible to treat it as if we're talking to another person. The system uses words like "I" and "believe" and "know," and it produces fluent, apparently thoughtful responses. So we naturally reach for the same folk-psychological vocabulary we use with each other, and we start attributing beliefs, desires, understanding, even feelings.

The problem is that those words carry an enormous amount of baggage. When I say that a person "knows" that Burundi is in Africa, that knowledge sits within a whole web of capacities: they can act on it, check it against the world, revise it if they encounter new evidence, and they're embedded in a shared world with other speakers. A bare language model is doing something quite different. At bottom, it's predicting the next token given a context, based on a vast corpus of human-generated text. When we ask it a question, what's actually happening is something more like, "Given the statistical distribution of human language, what words are likely to follow this sequence?" That's a very different thing from what a human is doing when they answer the same question.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying these systems are trivial, or that "it's just next-token prediction" settles everything. That would be a mistake in the other direction. The capabilities that emerge from that objective at scale are genuinely remarkable and surprising. The point is that we need to be precise about what's going on, and the anthropomorphic vocabulary tends to smuggle in assumptions we haven't earned.

One framing I've found useful is to think of the model as engaged in role-play. The underlying model is a kind of simulator that can play many characters, and the helpful assistant persona is one such character. When the character says "I believe X," it's tempting to take that at face value, but it may be more accurate to say the model is producing what that character would plausibly say. That helps explain things that look puzzling under a straightforwardly anthropomorphic reading, like so-called hallucination or apparent deception. The system isn't lying in the human sense; it's generating a plausible continuation in a role.

And the stakes aren't only philosophical. If people over-attribute understanding, they may trust these systems inappropriately, in medicine, say, or law. If people dismiss them entirely, they may miss real capabilities and real risks. So I think the right attitude is a kind of disciplined vigilance: we can use intentional language as a convenient shorthand, as people sometimes do with "the thermostat wants the room warmer," but we should keep reminding ourselves what these systems actually are and how they work, and not let the shorthand lead us astray.

r001.rationale: The response says dismissing AI entirely can cause people to miss real capabilities, but it does not state that anthropomorphism causes that underestimation.

r002.rationale: It says fluent, person-like language leads people to use human folk-psychological concepts and attribute beliefs, desires, and understanding to the system.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts language-model processing with human knowledge, but does not state that AI strengths and weaknesses across tasks differ sharply from the human pattern.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a very natural thing for us to do. We're wired to see minds everywhere, to attribute beliefs and desires and intentions to things that behave in even vaguely human-like ways. And of course large language models are the ultimate trigger for that tendency, because they produce fluent language, and language is the thing we most closely associate with having a mind. So when a chatbot says "I think" or "I feel" or "I understand," it's almost irresistible to take that at face value.

The trouble is that the folk psychological vocabulary we use for each other, words like belief, knowledge, understanding, intention, carries a whole lot of baggage with it. When I say that you believe it's raining, I'm implicitly assuming you can go and look out the window, that you'd be surprised if you got wet when you walked outside, that you'd adjust your behaviour accordingly. There's a whole web of connections to perception and action and embodiment that gives those words their meaning. A bare language model doesn't have any of that. It's a statistical model of text, trained to predict the next token, and that's a very strange kind of entity, something we've never really encountered before.

So the distortion works in both directions, actually. On the one hand, people overattribute. They assume that because the thing talks like us, it must have inner states like ours, it must understand in the way we understand, it must have something like a self with a continuous perspective on the world. And that leads to all sorts of confusion, about trust, about whether the system can be relied upon to know when it's wrong, about moral status even. On the other hand, there's a kind of reactive underattribution, where people say "it's just predicting the next word, so there's nothing interesting going on." And that's also a mistake, because the question of what's going on inside these systems is genuinely open, and the capabilities really are remarkable.

What I've tried to argue is that we should be careful with the language. Not that we should ban ourselves from ever saying a model "knows" something, that would be hopelessly impractical, and the shorthand is useful. But we should be conscious that we're using the words in an extended or metaphorical sense, and we should be prepared to cash them out in terms of what the system actually does. One way I've found helpful is to think of the model as role-playing, or as a kind of superposition of many possible characters that it can simulate. The base model isn't an "I" at all. When it says "I," it's generating the kind of thing a character would say, and the fine-tuning shapes which characters are favoured. That framing lets you take the behaviour seriously without importing the whole metaphysics of a unified human self.

The deeper point is that these systems sit somewhere in what I've called the space of possible minds, and they occupy a region we haven't got good concepts for yet. Our existing vocabulary evolved for dealing with other humans and, to a lesser extent, animals. It's not obvious it carves this new territory at the joints. So I think there's real conceptual work to be done, and anthropomorphism is a problem precisely because it short-circuits that work. It gives us the comforting illusion that we already understand what these things are, when actually we should be sitting with the strangeness for a while longer.

r001.rationale: The response describes “reactive underattribution” in people who dismiss a model as merely predicting the next word, then says that view is mistaken because the systems’ capabilities are remarkable.

r002.rationale: It says fluent language triggers mind attribution and that people assume a system that talks like us must understand as humans do and have human-like inner states.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe sharp differences between AI and human competence across tasks.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the first thing to acknowledge is how difficult it is to avoid. When something responds fluently in language, we naturally bring to it all the habits we’ve developed for interacting with other people. We say it knows something, it believes something, it wants to help. And almost without noticing, we start importing a whole picture of a mind behind the words.

The danger is that the language can get ahead of the evidence. If a language model says, “I’m confused,” that utterance doesn’t, by itself, establish that it’s experiencing confusion in the way a person does. Equally, if it gives a very convincing explanation, we shouldn’t automatically assume that the explanation faithfully describes how it arrived at its answer.

I find it helpful to keep moving between two perspectives. We can engage with the system conversationally, because that’s a useful way to interact with it. But we should also step back and remember how it was trained, what information it has access to, and what process is producing the response. In the case of a language model, generating a plausible continuation of a conversation can include playing the role of someone with beliefs, intentions, and feelings.

That doesn’t mean its capabilities are trivial, or that we should rule out every cognitive description. The point is to distinguish the capabilities we can actually demonstrate from the human characteristics we’re inclined to project onto them. Otherwise, the fluency of the performance can make us overlook some quite striking differences—and some quite surprising limitations.

r001.rationale: The response says anthropomorphism can obscure differences and limitations, but does not state that it causes people to underestimate capabilities the AI actually has.

r002.rationale: It says fluent language prompts people to apply habits from interacting with other people and to import a human-like picture of a mind behind the words, extending expectations beyond the language itself.

r003.rationale: The response mentions striking differences and limitations, but does not describe task-by-task strengths and weaknesses that differ sharply from the human pattern of competence.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to acknowledge is that it’s very difficult to avoid. When something converses fluently, we naturally reach for words like “knows,” “believes,” and “understands.” Those words are useful shorthand, but they bring a lot of baggage from our experience of other human beings.

If a person gives you a good answer to a question, you generally assume there’s a fairly stable set of beliefs behind it, and that they can draw on those beliefs in other circumstances. With a language model, that inference isn’t automatically justified. A convincing answer can lead us to attribute a coherent perspective, intentions, or an understanding that extends well beyond what we’ve actually tested.

But I wouldn’t want to go to the opposite extreme and dismiss its capabilities simply because the mechanism is different from ours. These systems can do remarkable things. The question is how to describe those abilities accurately, without importing an entire human psychology along with the description. We need to look carefully at what they can do, where they fail, and how sensitive their behaviour is to the context in which we ask them to perform.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against dismissing AI capabilities because its mechanism differs from ours, but does not say anthropomorphism causes people to underestimate those capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says fluent conversation leads people to use human terms and infer stable beliefs, intentions, or broader understanding that may not be justified.

r003.rationale: It mentions examining what models can do and where they fail, but does not state that their strengths and weaknesses across tasks differ sharply from the human pattern.
